entries.title: Makers and Takers: The Economics of the Kalshi Prediction Market
entries.authors_org: Constantin Bürgi; Wanying Deng; Karl Whelan (UCD)
entries.type: working_paper (CEPR DP20631 / GWU WP 2026-001; PDF version Jan 2026)
entries.claim: Kalshi 2021-Apr 2025, >300,000 contracts (46,282 markets, min $1,000 volume): clear favourite-longshot bias; contracts <10c lose >60% after fees; contracts >50c earn small positive returns; Makers earn far more than Takers; bias possibly diminishing over time.
entries.quote: average return on contracts for Makers was -9.64% while for Takers it was -31.46%
entries.effect_size: average return all contracts about -20% (pre-fee, volume-weighted); Makers -9.64% vs Takers -31.46% (post-fee); Makers buying >=50c: +2.6%; <10c: loss >60%
entries.net_of_costs: yes for Takers (taker fee 0.07*P*(1-P) included); Makers paid no fee in sample (Kalshi began charging makers after April 2025)
entries.capacity_note: not addressed; positive maker returns are small relative to taker losses; per-contract fee rounding; capacity UNKNOWN
entries.data_needed: per-contract trade prints with maker/taker side, prices, outcomes; Kalshi is a new external host
entries.advantage_class: 1 (documented, but only for Makers buying >=50c under the pre-April-2025 fee schedule)

entries.title: The Favorite-Longshot Bias in Prediction Markets: Evidence from Polymarket
entries.claim: 588 million trades by 2.48 million Polymarket accounts: aggregate favourite-longshot bias, but magnitude depends on aggregation; sign of longshot result flips when grouped by parent event; absent in sports; robust in crypto and politics.
entries.quote: lose 19.3 cents per dollar
entries.effect_size: purchases <10c lose 19.3 cents per dollar; purchases >=90c earn 0.83 cents; equal-weighted longshots -6.3c; event-grouped longshots +4.1c
entries.capacity_note: UNKNOWN; heavy favourite buyers (top decile) earn less than others
entries.data_needed: Polymarket trade history with outcomes; lab collects Polymarket books via pm_lp/pm_scanner (governed by pm_lp holdout rules; not read here)
entries.advantage_class: 2 (gross effect only; sign unstable under aggregation)

entries.title: Decomposing Crowd Wisdom: Domain-Specific Calibration Dynamics in Prediction Markets
entries.claim: 353 million trades, 429,000 binary contracts on Kalshi and Polymarket: calibration is conditional on domain, horizon and trade size; most robust pattern is political-market underconfidence (prices compressed toward 50%), replicated on Polymarket; roughly half of raw slope variation is estimation noise.
entries.quote: Calibration is therefore conditional
entries.effect_size: decomposition explains 87.3% of in-sample variance (Kalshi), 71.5% out-of-sample; large political trades slope gap ~0.5 (Kalshi, not robust on Polymarket)
entries.data_needed: contract-level prices by domain/horizon and outcomes
entries.advantage_class: 2 (calibration gap, not a tested trading result)

entries.title: Trading volume and liquidity provision in cryptocurrency markets
entries.authors_org: Daniele Bianchi; Mykola Babiak; Alexander Dickerson
entries.type: working_paper (Sveriges Riksbank WP 413, May 2022; also CERGE-EI WP 730)
entries.claim: USD pairs on multiple CEXs Mar 2017-Mar 2022: returns to liquidity provision (short-term reversal) concentrate in low-activity, smaller, more volatile, less liquid pairs. With a fixed 30/40 bp cost the equal-weighted reversal stays significant, but no value-weighted strategy is positive and significant, and alphas lose significance.
entries.quote: the alphas drastically decrease and are no longer statistically significant
entries.effect_size: EW reversal conditional on low volume 1.26%/day vs 0.54% high volume (gross); EW standard reversal after 30/40 bp costs 1.68%/day; VW low-volume reversal 0.65%/day gross; VW net: none significant
entries.net_of_costs: partly: fixed 30 bp long / 40 bp short; real micro-cap spreads not modelled
entries.capacity_note: effect lives in the smallest pairs; value-weighting kills it -> capacity tiny; equal-weight daily turnover

entries.advantage_class: 3 (equal-weight gross survives a flat 30-40 bp but value-weighted net fails; real spreads in illiquid pairs likely exceed the assumed cost)

entries.title: Day trading for a living?
entries.authors_org: Fernando Chague; Bruno Giovannetti; Rodrigo De-Losso
entries.claim: All individuals who started day trading Brazilian equity futures 2013-2015 and persisted >=300 days: 97% lost money; 0.4% earned more than a bank teller; no evidence of learning.
entries.effect_size: 97% lost money; best trader ~US$310/day with sd ~US$2,560

entries.title: The Big Picture: Journeying into Exotic Markets (Diary of a Quant 2)
entries.authors_org: Russell Korgaonkar (CIO Man AHL), Man Group
entries.claim: Man AHL trades >400 markets beyond traditional futures for differentiated alpha; cat bonds judged unsuitable for trend (intermittent trading, wide spreads); crypto initially shelved because exchanges and AML/KYC were inadequate; hard-to-access is not the same as illiquid.
entries.quote: just because a market is hard to access, it does not mean it is illiquid
entries.effect_size: n/a
entries.capacity_note: big firm does trade 'exotic' markets but requires daily tradability and institutional-grade venues
entries.conflict_of_interest: Man Group marketing its own capabilities
entries.advantage_class: shows what large firms avoid: venues failing KYC/AML/operational standards; markets without daily liquidity
